The piccolo oboe, also called the piccoloboe or sopranino oboe and formerly the oboe musette, is the smallest and highest member of the oboe family; it is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 422.112-71. It sounds an E♭ or an F above the ordinary oboe, and is written a minor third or a perfect fourth below its actual pitch, so it can be seen as the highest version of the oboe. It is most often found in military band music of the early twentieth century, and less often in chamber ensembles or contemporary works; it also appears in double-reed ensembles and in film scores.

As the smallest member of the oboe family it quickly found favour with band conductors for its bright, sharp timbre. In the early twentieth century it reached its height in marching and military bands, where it became indispensable. Its E♭ or F pitch let it cut easily through the band's heavy texture and strengthen the high part. As modern scoring changed, its use declined, and it is now rare in chamber and contemporary classical music. In the tradition of marching-band music, however, it keeps an important historical place and a special value.
